title: Rethinking Model Aggregation for Federated Learning with Domain Skew: A Knowledge-Preserving Perspective

paper.title: Rethinking Model Aggregation for Federated Learning with Domain Skew: A Knowledge-Preserving Perspective
paper.abstract: Abstract Domain skew challenges federated learning by requiring a shared model to accommodate distinct visual distributions. Domain-specific experts can capture these distributions separately, creating an opportunity to integrate their representations in a unified predictor. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), a two-stage framework that combines domain-oriented expert training with prototype-based classifier calibration. First, a one-shot subspace-based clustering procedure groups clients for intra-cluster training. The resulting expert encoders are concatenated and frozen, preserving each learned feature mapping during global integration. Second, clients interpolate their concatenated features with class-matched domain prototypes and upload the resulting virtual features. The server trains a global linear classifier on these features, concentrating classifier optimization at the server after a single feature upload. FKPL achieves average accuracies of 73.01%, 67.00%, and 64.51% on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and a four-domain subset of DomainNet, respectively. On DomainNet, its cross-domain standard deviation is 7.50 percentage points, the lowest among the evaluated methods. With the same concatenated extractor, prototype-based calibration improves average accuracy over federated classifier training by 9.99 and 14.94 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and PACS. These results identify classifier calibration as an effective way to combine preserved domain representations into a global predictor.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Federated learning (FL) enables distributed data owners to train models collaboratively while retaining their raw training samples locally [ 17 ] . Its applications include image classification [ 12 ] , medical analysis [ 1 ] , and Internet-of-Things systems [ 7 ] . A typical classification model combines a feature encoder, which maps an input to a representation vector, with a classifier, which converts that representation into class predictions. How to aggregate these components becomes consequential when clients observe different domains. Data heterogeneity creates differences between local objectives and their optimization trajectories [ 18 , 34 ] . Under domain skew, clients share a classification task while the appearance or acquisition conditions of their inputs vary [ 16 , 3 ] . A feature useful in one domain can receive conflicting updates from another domain. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting gap between a shared FedAvg model and independently trained domain models. This motivates an aggregation strategy that retains specialized representations while supporting a common prediction interface. Figure 1 : Federated learning across multiple domains. The reported domain accuracies compare FedAvg with domain-specific independent training (SOLO), illustrating the performance gap that motivates preserving specialized representations. Clustered FL groups clients with similar distributions and trains a model within each group [ 28 , 9 ] . This provides a direct route to domain specialization. Integrating the resulting experts requires an additional mechanism that combines their learned information. Shared-parameter approaches pursue global integration during training through regularization, partial parameter sharing, or modified aggregation [ 21 , 3 ] . When domain objectives conflict, their shared representations must accommodate competing requirements [ 20 , 2 ] . These observations motivate separating expert training from the construction of the final global classifier. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), following a “divide-and-integrate” design. Its first component, Domain Expert Training and Feature Aggregation (DETFA), applies one-shot subspace-based clustering [ 30 ] , trains experts within the resulting clusters, and concatenates their feature encoders. Freezing these encoders retains their learned mappings during the integration stage. Every input is then represented by the outputs of all experts, giving a common feature space for global prediction. The second component, Prototype-based Classifier Calibration (PCC), learns how to use this concatenated representation. Clients first compute class prototypes in the frozen global feature space. The server aggregates these prototypes within each cluster and distributes the resulting domain prototypes. Clients then interpolate local features with class-matched prototypes from the represented domains and upload the synthesized virtual features. The server uses this feature collection to train a global linear classifier. This arrangement moves the iterative classifier optimization to the server and makes the classifier’s access to cross-domain feature statistics explicit. Feature concatenation has an established role in FL. FedConcat [ 5 ] clusters clients using label-distribution information, trains cluster models, concatenates their encoders, and trains a classifier with the encoders frozen. FKPL develops this structural approach for domain-skewed data through two choices: client grouping based on data subspaces and classifier calibration using prototype-guided virtual features. The distinction lies in the grouping information and calibration protocol. Table 1 places these mechanisms alongside representative alternatives. Experiments on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and Domain-Net4 examine global prediction, component contributions, representation inversion, and system cost. The strongest component-level gains arise from PCC: with the concatenated extractor fixed, it increases average accuracy by 9.99 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and 14.94 points on PACS relative to a federated classifier. FKPL also produces the smallest cross-domain accuracy dispersion on Domain-Net4. These findings support the following contributions: 1. A domain-oriented integration framework combines subspace-based client grouping, intra-cluster expert training, and frozen encoder concatenation to retain specialized feature mappings in a global predictor. 2. Prototype-based classifier calibration constructs cross-domain virtual features in a common representation space and trains the global classifier at the server after a single feature-upload phase. 3. Experiments quantify the gains from classifier calibration, the contributions of expert grouping, and the communication and inference costs of retaining multiple encoders. Section 2 reviews the relevant FL approaches. Section 3 presents FKPL, Section 4 reports the experiments, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

sections.heading: 2.2 Learning with Heterogeneous Data
sections.text: Differences between client distributions can produce local updates that favor different representations [ 6 ] . FedProx constrains local updates using a proximal term [ 22 ] , while MOON regularizes representation learning through a model-contrastive objective [ 21 ] . Such methods modify the optimization of a shared model. Several approaches explicitly address domain skew. FCCL uses cross-correlation and knowledge distillation to transfer intra-domain and inter-domain information [ 15 ] . FPL uses clustered prototypes to guide representation learning [ 16 ] . FedHEAL combines partial parameter updates with fairness-aware aggregation to improve performance across domains [ 3 ] . Filter-aware relationships and personalized local structures offer another way to organize heterogeneous representations [ 33 ] . FKPL retains separate expert encoders and learns a classifier over their combined outputs, making structural preservation part of the aggregation procedure.

sections.heading: 2.3 Clustered Learning and Encoder Concatenation
sections.text: Clustered FL organizes clients according to their similarity. Examples use gradient similarity [ 28 ] , model divergence [ 24 ] , data-subspace principal angles [ 30 ] , or active-learning indicators [ 13 ] . PACFL extracts subspace information once before training and uses it to form client groups [ 30 ] . FKPL adopts this type of grouping to train domain-oriented experts. FedConcat provides a closely related encoder-integration mechanism [ 5 ] . It groups clients using label-distribution information, trains models within clusters, concatenates the trained encoders, and freezes them during federated classifier training. This establishes encoder concatenation as an existing FL mechanism. FKPL combines subspace-based domain grouping with server-side classifier calibration on virtual features formed from local representations and domain prototypes.

sections.heading: 2.4 Prototype Learning
sections.text: A class prototype summarizes feature vectors through a representative centroid [ 29 ] . FedProto and FedProc use prototypes to guide local training under heterogeneous data [ 29 , 26 ] , while RUCR uses unified prototypes to address classifier bias under long-tailed distributions [ 14 ] . FKPL computes class prototypes separately for each cluster in the same concatenated feature space. These prototypes guide interpolation during classifier calibration, connecting domain-level summaries with sample-level representations.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: FKPL combines domain-specific representation learning with a shared prediction rule. Domain Expert Training and Feature Aggregation (DETFA) learns separate encoders within client clusters and retains their outputs in a concatenated representation. Prototype-based Classifier Calibration (PCC) then trains a global classifier on synthesized features while keeping all encoders fixed.

sections.heading: 3.2 Motivation: Preserving Domain-Specific Representations
sections.text: Parameter sharing and clustered training provide different ways to use heterogeneous data. A shared encoder combines information across clients, while clustered training allows separate encoders to specialize in different distributions. The challenge addressed by FKPL is to combine these specialized representations into one predictor whose parameters can be deployed across the participating domains. Figure 2 : t-SNE visualization of PACS representations. The top row shows independently trained domain models; the bottom row shows the shared FedAvg model. The differences in class separation motivate retaining domain-specific encoders when constructing a unified predictor. An exploratory study on PACS [ 19 ] illustrates this motivation. Four clients each hold data from one domain and train a ResNet-10 model [ 11 ] . Figure 2 compares t-SNE embeddings [ 31 ] of penultimate-layer features after 100 epochs of independent training and 100 communication rounds of FedAvg. Independently trained models exhibit clearer class separation in several domains, particularly Sketch. This observation motivates a structural aggregation strategy that retains each trained encoder and learns how to combine its features with those of other domain experts.

sections.heading: 3.4 Threat Model and Privacy Evaluation Scope
sections.text: Information Available to the Server. We consider an honest-but-curious server that follows the protocol and can inspect client subspace summaries, uploaded expert parameters, local class prototypes, and labelled virtual features. It also knows the global extractor and the aggregated domain prototypes. Raw input samples remain on clients. The representation-inversion experiment in Section 4.4 measures reconstruction quality from the exchanged feature representations using the frozen global extractor. Information Available to a Participating Client. An in-cluster adversary knows its own data and prototypes, the shared cluster model, the global extractor, and the broadcast domain prototypes. For a class present at more than one client in its cluster, it can subtract its own contribution from the equal-client aggregate to recover the average prototype of the other contributing clients. The client-side evaluation measures reconstruction from this derived statistic. Subspace summaries, prototypes, and virtual features expose different levels of sample and class information. Prototype averaging and stochastic interpolation alter the reconstruction targets, and their effects are assessed through the specified inversion experiments. The reported reconstruction measurements characterize these observation and attack models.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets and client allocation. We evaluate FKPL on three multi-domain image-classification benchmarks. Office-Caltech-10 has ten classes in each of four domains: Caltech, Amazon, Webcam, and DSLR [ 8 ] . PACS contains seven classes across Photo, Art Painting, Cartoon, and Sketch [ 19 ] . Domain-Net4 is a subset of DomainNet [ 27 ] formed by selecting ten classes and using Clipart, Painting, Real, and Sketch. Sampling up to 200 images per class and domain gives 7,914 images: 1,914 from Clipart and 2,000 from each remaining domain. The experiments use 10 clients for Office-Caltech-10, 20 for PACS, and 10 for Domain-Net4. Each client draws its data from one domain. Domain-level training and test pools follow an 80/20 split. The domain allocations and local sampling ratios are specified in Table A1 . Client counts and sampling fractions vary across domains to represent different participation levels. The reported local sample counts range from 112 to 268 on Office-Caltech-10, from 98 to 214 on PACS, and from 400 to 1,600 on Domain-Net4, with means of 189, 156, and 618 samples per client, respectively. All methods use the same client allocation and held-out test pools for each benchmark. Models and comparisons. The base model uses a ResNet-10 encoder [ 11 ] and a linear classifier, following the backbone configuration used in multi-domain FL studies [ 16 , 3 ] . Each encoder outputs d = 512 d=512 features. With V = 4 V=4 experts, FKPL has a 2,048-dimensional concatenated representation. The classifier outputs seven logits for PACS and ten for the other datasets. We compare FKPL with twelve published methods: FedAvg [ 25 ] , FedProx [ 22 ] , MOON [ 21 ] , FedProc [ 26 ] , FedProto [ 29 ] , FPL [ 16 ] , FedHEAL [ 3 ] , FedRC [ 9 ] , FedBR [ 10 ] , FedGMKD [ 36 ] , FDSE [ 32 ] , and FedConcat [ 5 ] . Two additional architecture controls examine encoder width and grouping. FedAvg-Wide uses a single encoder with output dimension V ​ d Vd and trains it using FedAvg. Federated training runs for T = 100 T=100 rounds with full client participation, E = 10 E=10 local epochs, and batch size 64. Evaluation metrics. Let A i ∈ [ 0,100 ] A_{i}\in[0,100] be the reported accuracy, expressed as a percentage, on domain i i , and let D D be the number of evaluated domains. The summary metrics are AVG = 1 D ​ ∑ i = 1 D A i , \operatorname{AVG}=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=1}^{D}A_{i}, (13) STD = 1 D − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 D ( A i − AVG ) 2 . \operatorname{STD}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{D-1}\sum_{i=1}^{D}\bigl(A_{i}-\operatorname{AVG}\bigr)^{2}}. sections.heading: 4.3.3 Personalized Classifiers
sections.text: The frozen concatenated extractor also supports cluster-specific prediction heads. Clients in the same cluster can jointly train a classifier on their local samples using FedAvg while retaining the shared extractor. Each cluster-specific head improves the corresponding domain accuracy relative to the unified FKPL head. The same collection of preserved features therefore supports both a common prediction rule and classifiers adapted to individual clusters. sections.heading: 4.4 Representation Inversion Evaluation
sections.text: We examine reconstruction from four representations: raw features, local prototypes, aggregated prototypes, and virtual features. For each target, the attacker optimizes a 32 × 32 32\times 32 image by matching the target representation through the frozen global extractor. Adam runs for 800 steps with learning rate 0.05, total-variation regularization weight 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and L 2 L_{2} regularization weight 10 − 6 10^{-6} . Table 7 reports PSNR, SSIM, and the final feature-matching loss. Lower PSNR and SSIM indicate lower similarity to the reference image under this reconstruction procedure. Virtual features yield the lowest PSNR and SSIM among the four tested representations on both benchmarks. sections.text: Communication accounting. Table 9 counts the model-parameter and representation scalars exchanged by each component of the protocol. The size of the virtual-feature upload depends on N g N_{g} and the feature dimension d ​ V dV . sections.text: Let N = ∑ m = 1 M N m N=\sum_{m=1}^{M}N_{m} , let d x d_{x} be the vectorized input dimension, and let p p bound the number of retained subspace vectors per client. Denote the cost of extracting client m m ’s singular vectors by C SVD , m C_{\mathrm{SVD},m} . For a dense SVD of a d x × n d_{x}\times n class-data matrix, the arithmetic cost is 𝒪 ⁡ ( d x ​ n ​ min ⁡ { d x , n } ) \mathcal{O}(d_{x}n\min\{d_{x},n\}) ; truncated solvers have solver-dependent costs. Principal-angle comparisons can be computed from orthonormal bases of the uploaded spans. (17) The dense client-dissimilarity matrix requires 𝒪 ⁡ ( M 2 ) \mathcal{O}(M^{2}) storage. The clustering term explicitly includes the agglomeration step in addition to pairwise distance construction. With full client participation, T T communication rounds, and E E local epochs, the total expert-training work is 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ E ​ N ​ C train ) \mathcal{O}(TENC_{\mathrm{train}}) . This expression measures aggregate computation across clients; elapsed runtime also depends on client parallelism. PCC follows expert training. Let C enc C_{\mathrm{enc}} be the per-sample inference cost of one encoder, so evaluating the concatenated extractor costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( V ​ C enc ) \mathcal{O}(VC_{\mathrm{enc}}) . Let N g = | 𝒢 | N_{g}=|\mathcal{G}| be the number of uploaded virtual features, counted with their multiplicities. With cached local representations, feature extraction, prototype aggregation, feature synthesis, and R R epochs of linear-classifier training together cost 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ​ V ​ C enc + M ​ K ​ d ​ V + N g ​ d ​ V + R ​ N g ​ K ​ d ​ V ) . \mathcal{O}\!\left(NVC_{\mathrm{enc}}+MKdV+N_{g}dV+RN_{g}KdV\right). (18) When each example is mixed with one prototype from every cluster, N g = N ​ V N_{g}=NV ; missing class prototypes reduce this count according to the sets 𝒱 k \mathcal{V}_{k} . The global head contains K ​ d ​ V + K KdV+K parameters. Inference evaluates V V encoders and one linear head, giving per-sample cost 𝒪 ⁡ ( V ​ C enc + K ​ d ​ V ) \mathcal{O}(VC_{\mathrm{enc}}+KdV) . These expressions distinguish the one-time calibration workload from the recurring cost of deploying the concatenated extractor.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: FKPL integrates domain-specialized encoders into a unified predictor through feature concatenation and prototype-based classifier calibration. Subspace-based grouping organizes expert training around data distributions, while virtual-feature synthesis supplies the server with calibration examples guided by domain prototypes. Experiments on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and Domain-Net4 show improvements over FedAvg and identify classifier calibration as a major source of the gains. On Domain-Net4, FKPL also attains the lowest cross-domain accuracy dispersion among the evaluated methods. This combination of modular representation learning and server-side calibration provides a design for federated classification across participating domains. Future work will explore expert selection and representation compression to reduce deployment costs.

Address: Cyberspace Institute of Advanced Technology, Guangzhou University, Guangzhou 510006, China Abstract Domain skew challenges federated learning by requiring a shared model to accommodate distinct visual distributions. Domain-specific experts can capture these distributions separately, creating an opportunity to integrate their representations in a unified predictor. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), a two-stage framework that combines domain-oriented expert training with prototype-based classifier calibration. First, a one-shot subspace-based clustering procedure groups clients for intra-cluster training. The resulting expert encoders are concatenated and frozen, preserving each learned feature mapping during global integration. Second, clients interpolate their concatenated features with class-matched domain prototypes and upload the resulting virtual features. The server trains a global linear classifier on these features, concentrating classifier optimization at the server after a single feature upload. FKPL achieves average accuracies of 73.01%, 67.00%, and 64.51% on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and a four-domain subset of DomainNet, respectively. On DomainNet, its cross-domain standard deviation is 7.50 percentage points, the lowest among the evaluated methods. With the same concatenated extractor, prototype-based calibration improves average accuracy over federated classifier training by 9.99 and 14.94 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and PACS. These results identify classifier calibration as an effective way to combine preserved domain representations into a global predictor. Keywords: Model aggregation , federated learning , domain skew , classifier calibration , feature concatenation 1 Introduction Federated learning (FL) enables distributed data owners to train models collaboratively while retaining their raw training samples locally [ 17 ] . Its applications include image classification [ 12 ] , medical analysis [ 1 ] , and Internet-of-Things systems [ 7 ] . A typical classification model combines a feature encoder, which maps an input to a representation vector, with a classifier, which converts that representation into class predictions. How to aggregate these components becomes consequential when clients observe different domains. Data heterogeneity creates differences between local objectives and their optimization trajectories [ 18 , 34 ] . Under domain skew, clients share a classification task while the appearance or acquisition conditions of their inputs vary [ 16 , 3 ] . A feature useful in one domain can receive conflicting updates from another domain. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting gap between a shared FedAvg model and independently trained domain models. This motivates an aggregation strategy that retains specialized representations while supporting a common prediction interface. Figure 1 : Federated learning across multiple domains. The reported domain accuracies compare FedAvg with domain-specific independent training (SOLO), illustrating the performance gap that motivates preserving specialized representations. Clustered FL groups clients with similar distributions and trains a model within each group [ 28 , 9 ] . This provides a direct route to domain specialization. Integrating the resulting experts requires an additional mechanism that combines their learned information. Shared-parameter approaches pursue global integration during training through regularization, partial parameter sharing, or modified aggregation [ 21 , 3 ] . When domain objectives conflict, their shared representations must accommodate competing requirements [ 20 , 2 ] . These observations motivate separating expert training from the construction of the final global classifier. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), following a “divide-and-integrate” design. Its first component, Domain Expert Training and Feature Aggregation (DETFA), applies one-shot subspace-based clustering [ 30 ] , trains experts within the resulting clusters, and concatenates their feature encoders. Freezing these encoders retains their learned mappings during the integration stage. Every input is then represented by the outputs of all experts, giving a common feature space for global prediction. The second component, Prototype-based Classifier Calibration (PCC), learns how to use this concatenated representation. Clients first compute class prototypes in the frozen global feature space. The server aggregates these prototypes within each cluster and distributes the resulting domain prototypes. Clients then interpolate local features with class-matched prototypes from the represented domains and upload the synthesized virtual features. The server uses this feature collection to train a global linear classifier. This arrangement moves the iterative classifier optimization to the server and makes the classifier’s access to cross-domain feature statistics explicit. Feature concatenation has an established role in FL. FedConcat [ 5 ] clusters clients using label-distribution information, trains cluster models, concatenates their encoders, and trains a classifier with the encoders frozen. FKPL develops this structural approach for domain-skewed data through two choices: client grouping based on data subspaces and classifier calibration using prototype-guided virtual features. The distinction lies in the grouping information and calibration protocol. Table 1 places these mechanisms alongside representative alternatives. Experiments on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and Domain-Net4 examine global prediction, component contributions, representation inversion, and system cost. The strongest component-level gains arise from PCC: with the concatenated extractor fixed, it increases average accuracy by 9.99 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and 14.94 points on PACS relative to a federated classifier. FKPL also produces the smallest cross-domain accuracy dispersion on Domain-Net4. These findings support the following contributions: 1. A domain-oriented integration framework combines subspace-based client grouping, intra-cluster expert training, and frozen encoder concatenation to retain specialized feature mappings in a global predictor. 2. Prototype-based classifier calibration constructs cross-domain virtual features in a common representation space and trains the global classifier at the server after a single feature-upload phase. 3. Experiments quantify the gains from classifier calibration, the contributions of expert grouping, and the communication and inference costs of retaining multiple encoders. Section 2 reviews the relevant FL approaches. Section 3 presents FKPL, Section 4 reports the experiments, and Section 5 concludes the paper. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Federated Learning Consider a server and M M clients. Client m m holds a dataset 𝒟 m = { ( 𝒙 m , i , y m , i ) } i = 1 N m \mathcal{D}_{m}=\{(\boldsymbol{x}_{m,i},y_{m,i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{m}} , where N m = | 𝒟 m | N_{m}=|\mathcal{D}_{m}| . With N = ∑ m = 1 M N m N=\sum_{m=1}^{M}N_{m} , the standard sample-weighted FL objective is min ⁡ ∑ m = 1 M w ⁡ N m N ​ ℒ m ​ ( w ) , ℒ m ​ ( w ) = 1 N m ​ ∑ i = 1 N m ℓ ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( 𝒙 m , i , w ) , y m , i ) , \min_{w}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{N_{m}}{N}\mathcal{L}_{m}(w),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{m}(w)=\frac{1}{N_{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{m}}\ell\bigl(f(\boldsymbol{x}_{m,i};w),y_{m,i}\bigr), (1) where f ⁡ ( ⋅ , w ) f(\cdot;w) is the model and ℓ \ell is the per-sample classification loss. FedAvg alternates local optimization with sample-weighted parameter aggregation [ 25 ] . 2.2 Learning with Heterogeneous Data Differences between client distributions can produce local updates that favor different representations [ 6 ] . FedProx constrains local updates using a proximal term [ 22 ] , while MOON regularizes representation learning through a model-contrastive objective [ 21 ] . Such methods modify the optimization of a shared model. Several approaches explicitly address domain skew. FCCL uses cross-correlation and knowledge distillation to transfer intra-domain and inter-domain information [ 15 ] . FPL uses clustered prototypes to guide representation learning [ 16 ] . FedHEAL combines partial parameter updates with fairness-aware aggregation to improve performance across domains [ 3 ] . Filter-aware relationships and personalized local structures offer another way to organize heterogeneous representations [ 33 ] . FKPL retains separate expert encoders and learns a classifier over their combined outputs, making structural preservation part of the aggregation procedure. 2.3 Clustered Learning and Encoder Concatenation Clustered FL organizes clients according to their similarity. Examples use gradient similarity [ 28 ] , model divergence [ 24 ] , data-subspace principal angles [ 30 ] , or active-learning indicators [ 13 ] . PACFL extracts subspace information once before training and uses it to form client groups [ 30 ] . FKPL adopts this type of grouping to train domain-oriented experts. FedConcat provides a closely related encoder-integration mechanism [ 5 ] . It groups clients using label-distribution information, trains models within clusters, concatenates the trained encoders, and freezes them during federated classifier training. This establishes encoder concatenation as an existing FL mechanism. FKPL combines subspace-based domain grouping with server-side classifier calibration on virtual features formed from local representations and domain prototypes. 2.4 Prototype Learning A class prototype summarizes feature vectors through a representative centroid [ 29 ] . FedProto and FedProc use prototypes to guide local training under heterogeneous data [ 29 , 26 ] , while RUCR uses unified prototypes to address classifier bias under long-tailed distributions [ 14 ] . FKPL computes class prototypes separately for each cluster in the same concatenated feature space. These prototypes guide interpolation during classifier calibration, connecting domain-level summaries with sample-level representations. 2.5 Comparison of Integration Mechanisms Table 1 compares concrete training and prediction mechanisms. FKPL uses clustering to construct specialized encoders and prototype-guided feature synthesis to fit a shared classifier. Its global prediction evaluates every expert on each input, so the classifier can combine their outputs without selecting a domain-specific model at inference time. A shared encoder combines information across clients, while clustered training allows separate encoders to specialize in different distributions. The challenge addressed by FKPL is to combine these specialized representations into one predictor whose parameters can be deployed across the participating domains. The differences in class separation motivate retaining domain-specific encoders when constructing a unified predictor. An exploratory study on PACS [ 19 ] illustrates this motivation. Four clients each hold data from one domain and train a ResNet-10 model [ 11 ] . Independently trained models exhibit clearer class separation in several domains, particularly Sketch. We consider an honest-but-curious server that follows the protocol and can inspect client subspace summaries, uploaded expert parameters, local class prototypes, and labelled virtual features. It also knows the global extractor and the aggregated domain prototypes. Raw input samples remain on clients. The representation-inversion experiment in Section 4.4 measures reconstruction quality from the exchanged feature representations using the frozen global extractor. Information Available to a Participating Client. An in-cluster adversary knows its own data and prototypes, the shared cluster model, the global extractor, and the broadcast domain prototypes. For a class present at more than one client in its cluster, it can subtract its own contribution from the equal-client aggregate to recover the average prototype of the other contributing clients. The client-side evaluation measures reconstruction from this derived statistic. Subspace summaries, prototypes, and virtual features expose different levels of sample and class information. Prototype averaging and stochastic interpolation alter the reconstruction targets, and their effects are assessed through the specified inversion experiments. The reported reconstruction measurements characterize these observation and attack models. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets and client allocation. We evaluate FKPL on three multi-domain image-classification benchmarks. Office-Caltech-10 has ten classes in each of four domains: Caltech, Amazon, Webcam, and DSLR [ 8 ] . PACS contains seven classes across Photo, Art Painting, Cartoon, and Sketch [ 19 ] . Domain-Net4 is a subset of DomainNet [ 27 ] formed by selecting ten classes and using Clipart, Painting, Real, and Sketch. Sampling up to 200 images per class and domain gives 7,914 images: 1,914 from Clipart and 2,000 from each remaining domain. The experiments use 10 clients for Office-Caltech-10, 20 for PACS, and 10 for Domain-Net4. Each client draws its data from one domain. Domain-level training and test pools follow an 80/20 split. The domain allocations and local sampling ratios are specified in Table A1 . Client counts and sampling fractions vary across domains to represent different participation levels. The reported local sample counts range from 112 to 268 on Office-Caltech-10, from 98 to 214 on PACS, and from 400 to 1,600 on Domain-Net4, with means of 189, 156, and 618 samples per client, respectively. All methods use the same client allocation and held-out test pools for each benchmark. Models and comparisons. The base model uses a ResNet-10 encoder [ 11 ] and a linear classifier, following the backbone configuration used in multi-domain FL studies [ 16 , 3 ] . Each encoder outputs d = 512 d=512 features. With V = 4 V=4 experts, FKPL has a 2,048-dimensional concatenated representation. The classifier outputs seven logits for PACS and ten for the other datasets. We compare FKPL with twelve published methods: FedAvg [ 25 ] , FedProx [ 22 ] , MOON [ 21 ] , FedProc [ 26 ] , FedProto [ 29 ] , FPL [ 16 ] , FedHEAL [ 3 ] , FedRC [ 9 ] , FedBR [ 10 ] , FedGMKD [ 36 ] , FDSE [ 32 ] , and FedConcat [ 5 ] . Two additional architecture controls examine encoder width and grouping. FedAvg-Wide uses a single encoder with output dimension V ​ d Vd and trains it using FedAvg. Ensemble-Independent retains the number and sizes of the FKPL groups and randomly reassigns clients to those groups. Training. Federated training runs for T = 100 T=100 rounds with full client participation, E = 10 E=10 local epochs, and batch size 64. Local optimization uses SGD with learning rate 0.01, momentum 0.9, and weight decay 10 − 5 10^{-5} . FKPL applies these settings within each cluster. Its one-shot average-linkage clustering returns four clusters for each benchmark, and the resulting partitions remain fixed across training runs. Inputs are resized to 32 × 32 32\times 32 . PCC trains the linear classifier for R = 200 R=200 epochs using the optimizer settings in A . The reported classification results are averages over five independent training runs with different random seeds, using a fixed train/test split. Hyperparameters are selected using validation data. The final global predictor is evaluated on held-out samples from every participating domain. Tables A1 and A2 summarize the shared training configuration and FKPL-specific settings.
